articles.summary: By Tyler Thomas, Engineering Manager In commercial AI, eighteen months is an eternity. Microarchitectures turn over, memory bandwidth doubles, and rack-level thermal envelopes are rewritten before the thermal paste on last year’s deployment has even dried. In aerospace and defense, eighteen months may not get you through preliminary design reviews and initial environmental screening. This cadence mismatch is the central dilemma of modern tactical computing: Defense programs often run on 5- to 10-year lifecycles, but modern edge processing operates on an 18-month commercial silicon clock. If you design a mission system around a monolithic custom compute architecture, you are virtually guaranteed to field a legacy system. By the time an armored vehicle or an airborne ISR pod enters operational service, the deep neural networks it was intended to run have evolved past the compute capability of the silicon bolted inside it. Yet, simply buying commodity enterprise servers is typically a non-starter. A commercial datacenter box shaken on a tactical vehicle will shear connections, choke on dust, and succumb to dirty power transients within hours. articles.summary: By Fabrizio Sardo, Vice President of Operations To understand what it takes to manufacture a rugged computing system, it helps to start with something unlikely to appear in a product brochure: a thermal pad. On a drawing, the pad has a precise location; at the workbench, meeting that requirement involves cutting material, positioning it accurately, and assembling the surrounding components. During OSS assembly and cycle-time reviews, these routine tasks prompted questions about whether a cutting fixture or alignment guide might improve consistency, as well as how connector seating, tool access, and test sequencing could influence the build. Such details rarely appear in a product specification, yet they help determine whether instructions are clear, work is repeatable, and each person has what they need to do the job correctly. Our customers are understandably focused on performance, from processing and storage to cooling and operation outside the conventional data center, but delivering that capability requires coordination among Engineering, Operations, Quality, and the people who assemble and test OSS systems. The Work Starts Before the Workbench A production date on the schedule does not always mean an order is ready to build. Beyond material availability, planners must consider remaining work, assembly and test capacity, and repair activity that draws on the same people and equipment; Procurement must also account for supplier processes that affect when a part is ready for assembly. Consider a circuit board requiring conformal coating. Sending it to a processor is only one step, because the drawing must communicate coating and masking requirements, while Procurement, Engineering, and Quality need a shared understanding of the expected result before the board reaches assembly. That preparation is easy to overlook, but it helps make the production schedule credible. Rather than asking only whether an order is open or materials have arrived, our planning discussions focus on what must be true before the next operation begins, bringing materials, documentation, and floor capacity into the same conversation. Where Engineering Intent Meets Manufacturing Reality A drawing establishes what must be built, but it cannot capture everything an assembler encounters at the workbench. It may show exactly where a component belongs without revealing how easily someone can reach a fastener, handle a cable, or fully seat a connector, questions the people doing the work are often the first to raise. I see that feedback as an essential part of disciplined manufacturing, rather than a complaint to dismiss or permission to make unapproved changes. When questions reach the right technical owner and the resolution is reflected in the build information, everyone can work from the same approved understanding. Manufacturing engineering helps turn those observations into practical improvement opportunities by studying builds, cycle times, and tooling to identify ways to make work more consistent. Our thermal-pad review generated ideas such as a cutting fixture or alignment guide, but an idea must be evaluated before it becomes standard practice; proposing an improvement and demonstrating its value are not the same thing. The goal is a process people can understand, execute, and repeat without compromising the design. What It Takes to Call a System Ready A system may look complete when assembly ends, but readiness for delivery depends on more than its appearance. Depending on the configuration, setup and acceptance testing still must follow the applicable procedure, making test equipment, technician availability, and engineering support as important to scheduling as assembly capacity. When a test result needs investigation, Test, Engineering, Production, and Quality may each hold part of the answer. At the same time, the hardware configuration, applicable procedure, and recorded results must remain aligned; without that traceability, we cannot reliably establish what was tested and what was verified. Even a system that has passed testing may not be ready to ship, because packaging, release documentation, and customer-specific conditions still require attention. There are times when a shipment should be held while a requirement or document is clarified, and those decisions deserve the same care as earlier technical work. By the time a customer sees the completed system, the questions raised at the bench, the supplier requirements clarified upstream, and the test and release records reviewed are largely invisible. Although different teams make these decisions at different points, their combined judgment shapes what ultimately leaves our facility. I do not view Operations as the department that takes over once Engineering completes a design; our role is to help turn engineering intent into hardware that can be built consistently, tested appropriately, documented accurately, and delivered to the customer. That work depends on people throughout OSS whose contributions may never appear in a product launch, but whose judgment affects every build. Specifications describe what an OSS system is designed to do; the work behind the build is how we make that design ready to deliver. If you are developing a rugged edge computing application, connect with OSS to discuss its requirements and the practical work involved in taking it from design to delivery.

articles.summary: Strengthens OSS’s role in developing the U.S. Army’s next-generation tactical ground vehicle compute architecture Advanced compute system designed to support operational C5ISR integration and distribution Development award may provide opportunities for future production programs across multiple U.S. Army and allied vehicle platforms ESCONDIDO, Calif. – November 9, 2026 – One Stop Systems, Inc. (OSS or the Company) (Nasdaq: OSS), a leader in rugged Enterprise Class compute for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and sensor processing at the edge, today announced it has been awarded a $2.75 million contract by the U.S. Army to develop a next-generation compute appliance for tactical ground vehicles. This award reflects OSS’s multi-year efforts to integrate high-performance technology into the compute architecture of the Army’s tactical ground vehicles. OSS currently anticipates delivering working systems to the Army during the second half of 2027. Under the contract, OSS’s engineering team will work with the Army to develop a Sensor Open Systems Architecture (SOSA) aligned compute system in support of the U.S. Army’s near-term ground vehicle program office requirements. The latest award builds upon OSS’s ongoing work with the Army in developing its next-generation tactical ground vehicle compute architecture. It also extends OSS’s rugged AI compute technology into new mission critical defense applications, an increasingly critical priority for the U.S. Department of War. OSS believes the SOSA-aligned architecture may support potential applications across multiple U.S. Army and allied military vehicle platforms. “We are pleased to continue supporting the Army as it brings high-performance technology into the compute architecture of its tactical ground vehicles,” said Mike Knowles, President and CEO of OSS. “We believe this award reflects the strength of our rugged compute and sensor processing platforms and our ability to address the Army’s evolving requirements. Our experience across multiple defense and commercial programs demonstrates the potential for initial development awards to lead to meaningful production opportunities. We believe our early involvement in this program positions OSS to compete for follow-on orders as the program matures. It also furthers our strategy of taking our Enterprise Class compute deeper into next-generation defense programs.” About One Stop SystemsOne Stop Systems, Inc. (Nasdaq: OSS) is a leader in AI enabled solutions for the demanding 'edge'. OSS designs and manufactures Enterprise Class compute and storage products that enable rugged AI, sensor fusion and autonomous capabilities without compromise. These hardware and software platforms bring the latest data center performance to harsh and challenging applications, whether they are on land, sea or in the air. OSS products include ruggedized servers, compute accelerators, flash storage arrays, and storage acceleration software. These specialized compact products are used across multiple industries and applications, including autonomous trucking and farming, as well as aircraft, drones, ships and vehicles within the defense industry. OSS solutions address the overall AI workflow, from high-speed data acquisition to deep learning, training and large-scale inference, and have delivered many industry firsts for industrial OEM and government customers. As one of the fastest growing segments of the multi-billion-dollar edge computing market, AI enabled solutions require-and OSS delivers-the highest level of performance in the most challenging environments without compromise. OSS products are available directly or through global distributors. For more information, go to www.onestopsystems.com. You can also follow OSS on X, YouTube, and LinkedIn.
